785: (15) Something that was fully cooked and is dry with no broth in it may be placed opposite the fire even in a place where the hand is scalded. {Rama: And even if it already cooled. But if it is boiling, even something that has broth in it is permitted. And some are lenient to say that anything not placed directly on the fire or stove but only close to it — even if it cooled — is permitted (Maggid Mishneh chapter 22). And the custom is to be lenient in this if it has not completely cooled, and as I wrote above in siman 253.}
788: (38) 'It is permitted to place it opposite the fire' — for it is comparable to leaving it on a stove, which is permitted; and even though nothing intervenes between it and the fire, since the Sages required moving it somewhat away from the fire there is a recognizable distinction and he will not come to rake the coals — the Rosh.
790: (39) 'If it did not cool completely, it is permitted' — for he holds there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking even in broth that cooled.
792: (40) 'If it did not cool completely' — the reason is that there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking even in broth that cooled.
794: (47) 'Seif 15, something' — we learn from oil: according to the view that holds oil has no concern of cooking; and see seif 4 and seif 8.
796: (48) 'And even, etc., but' — as written in seif 4.
798: (6) 'Cooled' — see the Beer Heitev and see Rabbeinu Yonah in the name of Mahariv Tarani in a handwritten responsum, regarding what they were accustomed in Constantinople where the maidservants would place cholent and chicken to warm inside the oven.
800: (92) 'Something that was cooked, etc.' — the reason is that since it was already cooked there is no further concern of cooking. However on the fire itself it is forbidden by rabbinic law because it appears as if he is cooking.
802: (93) 'Fully cooked and dry' — for if not fully cooked, even if it is dry and hot, there is still a concern of cooking as stated above in seif 4.
804: (94) 'Opposite the fire' — he used the expression 'opposite the fire' and not 'beside the fire' to teach that one must move somewhat away from the fire, and therefore there is no concern that he will come to rake the coals.
806: (95) 'And even if it already cooled' — to explain the Mechaber's words: he is dealing with something that cooled, and therefore he only permitted a dry item.
810: (97) 'And some are lenient' — they disagree with the Mechaber, holding that specifically when it is dry is there no cooking after cooking; but a wet item that cooled has cooking after cooking. This opinion holds that there is no cooking after cooking at all.
812: (98) 'On top of the fire, etc.' — for if he places it directly, even though there is no Torah prohibition according to them, it is at least forbidden by rabbinic law because it appears as if he is cooking, and also lest he come to rake.
814: (99) 'If not, etc.' — even though the Mechaber holds that since it cooled somewhat from its heat and the hand is no longer scalded in it there is again a concern of cooking as written above in seif 4 — the custom is to be lenient as long as it has not completely cooled as written in siman 253.
816: (89) 'The hand is scalded in it' — since it is cooked and dry there is no Torah prohibition of cooking. And even though the Sages decreed and forbade placing it on the stove, they did not forbid placing it opposite the fire in this condition.
818: (90) 'It is permitted' — as long as the food is hot and yad soledes bo, according to all opinions there is no cooking.
820: (91) 'Just close to it' — and in that case there is no concern of appearing as a cook.
822: (92) 'Even if it cooled, it is permitted' — the Rama brings here the method of the rishonim that there is no cooking after cooking at all, even in a liquid. This opinion is very reasonable based on the Talmudic sources.
824: (93) 'If it has not completely cooled' — meaning: the Rama rules in principle like the lenient opinions, that it is permitted to heat food even if it has broth, as long as it has not completely cooled. But due to the importance of the matter the Rama writes that the custom is to be stringent.
826: (94) 'Siman 253' — at the end of seif 5, where the Rama writes that it is permitted to return a cooked pot to the fire as long as it is still warm.
829: 'And it is dry, etc., opposite the fire' — this requires investigation, for above in seif 5 he brings the opinion of the Ra'em, and see there in the Magen Avraham that according to his view the same applies that there is roasting after cooking — and how does he permit here simply [see Beit Me'ir on Orach Chayyim, and the book Maamar Mordechai also raised this difficulty].
